newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Rebel onslaught prompts Colombian security meeting.
newsitem.headline: Rebel onslaught prompts Colombian security meeting.

text.p: The Colombian government held a high-level security meeting on Tuesday to discuss ways of curbing a recent surge in leftist guerrilla activity across the country.

But the four-hour meeting at the Casa de Narino presidential palace, dubbed a "law and order summit" by President Ernesto Samper's official spokesman, ended with no specific announcements about possible ways of cracking down on Colombia's newly emboldened rebels.

The meeting involving Samper, his military chiefs, senior Cabinet officials and governors and mayors from provinces hardest hit by the guerrilla war, was held against the backdrop of a rebel offensive beginning in late August that killed more than 150 security force members and wounded hundreds.

Guerrillas also took more than 60 soldiers prisoner, blew up oil pipelines and paralyzed key roadways, burning trucks and blocking exports of coal and coffee in a spiral of attacks that caused tens of millions of dollars in economic losses.

Adding to widespread fears that the security situation threatened to spin out of control, authorities said on Friday they had uncovered rebel plans to launch a series of high-profile attacks in Bogota as part of a guerrilla effort to move their war from the countryside to the capital.

Government officials have said they were considering calling up Colombia's military reserves to confront what many agree to be the most dramatic offensive Colombia has seen in more than three decades of guerrilla war. No one has said where the cash-strapped government would come up with the money to pay for army reinforcements, however, and Tuesday's meeting ended with no word on a possible move to pour more troops into the countryside.

Guerrillas have fought under the banner of land reform for decades and the Agriculture Ministry confirmed in a statement on Tuesday that the government had prepared a decree allowing for the expropriation of large land holdings -- and their handover to landless peasants -- in areas torn by political bloodshed.

It remains to be seen how the decree calling for the creation of "peasant reservations" will be put into effect, however, and Interior Minister Horacio Serpa said the issue of land reform was barely touched on during the security meeting.

Mauricio Pimiento, governor of the rebel-infested northern province of Cesar, called the meeting a major disappointment since no specific measures were adopted to end the spiral of violence in the countryside.

Political analysts say Cesar is a prime example of the need for agrarian reform in Colombia since large landholders there, working together with right-wing paramilitary groups, have succeeded in driving tens of thousands of peasants off their own small parcels of land since the 1930s.
Guerrilla strength and crime in the province has grown proportionately with the number of landless and deeply impoverished peasants.

Serpa, in brief remarks to reporters during a recess in the closed-door meeting at the presidential palace, conceded that guerrillas have wreaked havoc across the country since late August. He ruled out any dramatic measures such as the declaration of a state of emergency, however, saying the public order situation appeared to be on the mend.
"The authorities have effective control over all areas of the country," he said. "We hope that the situation will continue improving in the immediate future."
